changes.after: Check whether a pattern matches the whole input or only part of it.

before: Regex("[0-9]+") describes one or more ASCII digits. The bracket expression selects one digit; + requires at least one repetition. This deliberately excludes signs and whitespace, and does not prove that the numeric value fits Int.
matches requires the whole input to match. containsMatchIn asks whether any matching substring exists. For x12, the digit substring exists even though the complete input is not all digits.

Complete local Kotlin/JVM example; the app itself does not execute it:
```kotlin


fun main() {
    val digits = Regex("[0-9]+")
    println(digits.matches("x12"))
    println(digits.containsMatchIn("x12"))
}
```

Expected output or behavior: false
true. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Compare an empty input and a signed number before choosing a validation policy. You may trace it without a Kotlin compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: A regular expression, or regex, is a pattern for matching text. In `[0-9]+`, the brackets allow a digit from 0 through 9. The plus sign requires one or more of those digits.
The function `matches` checks the whole input. The function `containsMatchIn` looks for any matching part inside it. These answer different questions.

Follow the example one line at a time.
```kotlin


fun main() {
    val digits = Regex("[0-9]+")
    println(digits.matches("x12"))
    println(digits.containsMatchIn("x12"))
}
```
The screen shows `false`, then `true`. The full text x12 is not all digits, but the part 12 matches the pattern.
This pattern does not accept a sign, spaces, or empty input as a whole match. Even a matching digit string might be too large for Int. A pattern check and a number-range check do different jobs.
